p.x:
Last Saturday, my friend Mint came to my house for a sleepover. We slept in my bunk bed. I was on the top, and Mint was on the bottom.
We watched a film and ate popcorn. At midnight, Mum came in and said, "Close the curtains and go to sleep!" But we weren't sleepy. We stayed awake and talked for a long time.
Finally, I fell asleep at about one o'clock. In the morning, Mint was still asleep, so I changed the sheets on my bed quietly. We were both very tired all day!

p.t: Are You an Early Bird or a Night Owl?
p.x:
Some people wake up early full of energy. They are early birds. Others feel most awake late at night. They are night owls. Scientists say this depends partly on your body clock, the natural rhythm that tells you when to sleep and wake.
Modern life makes good sleep difficult. Many people look at their phones in bed, but the blue light from screens tells the brain it is still daytime. As a result, they have a restless night, wake up groggy, or even oversleep and arrive late for work. Workers on the night shift find it especially hard, because they must sleep during the day.
There are simple ways to sleep better. Make your bedroom dark and quiet; an eye mask can help if your curtains are thin. A comfortable mattress and a warm duvet in winter also make a difference. An hour before bed, turn off screens and wind down with a book or some quiet music. If you doze off in the afternoon, keep the nap short, or you may not sleep at night. In some countries, such as Spain, a short siesta after lunch is traditional.
At weekends, many people like to lie in, but sleeping much later than usual can confuse your body. Most adults need seven to nine hours to feel well-rested. Sleep is when the body and brain recharge, so it is not wasted time. Bad dreams and the occasional nightmare are normal, and some children even sleepwalk, but these usually stop as they grow older. If you travel overnight, try to sleep on the plane.

For centuries, sleep was considered a passive state in which the body simply rested. Today, scientists know that the sleeping brain is remarkably active. Each night, we pass through several stages, and one complete sleep cycle lasts roughly ninety minutes. During deep sleep, the body repairs tissues and releases growth hormones, while REM sleep, named after the rapid eye movements that accompany it, is when most vivid dreaming occurs.
The timing of sleep is controlled largely by melatonin, a hormone released by the brain as darkness falls. Artificial light, particularly from screens, can delay this process, making it harder to fall asleep. Many people then toss and turn for hours, and a chronic insomniac may go weeks without a proper night's rest.
The effects of sleep deprivation are serious. Even a single short night can make people irritable and slow to react, and long-term lack of sleep has been linked to obesity, heart disease and depression. It also weakens the immune system, making us more likely to catch colds. Research suggests that sleep plays a vital role in learning: during the night, the brain appears to consolidate information acquired during the day, transforming short-term memories into long-term ones. Students who stay up all night before an exam may therefore be undermining their own performance.
Some sleep problems require medical attention. Sleep apnoea, a condition in which breathing repeatedly stops during the night, often goes undiagnosed, although loud snoring and daytime exhaustion are common warning signs.
